#7614. A surge in cases on religion and schools

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

Welcome to a new month and a new argument session. The justices will hear argument in seven cases over the next nine days.

Today, the justices will hear argument in two cases: Maxwell v. Dinis, on a federal inmate’s ability to use a habeas statute, 28 U.S.C. § 2241, to contest the Federal Bureau of Prisons’ refusal to accelerate his transfer to a halfway house or home confinement; and Younge v. Fulton Judicial Circuit District Attorney’s Office, Georgia, on whether an affirmative defense may be asserted as a basis for summary judgment if not presented earlier in a pleading.

On Tuesday, the justices will hear argument in St. Mary Catholic Parish v. Roy, a religious discrimination challenge brought by Catholic preschools in Colorado over the state’s requirement that all schools participating in its universal preschool program must admit everyone – including LGBTQ children and children with LGBTQ parents.

On Oct. 21, the Trump administration asked the justices to allow it to resume construction of its border wall in the Big Bend region of southwestern Texas. The request is now fully briefed, and the court’s decision could come at any time.

#7609. Lawyers’ AI use doesn’t justify slashing $115K fee award, appellate court says

A federal appeals court has rejected an argument that a law firm’s use of artificial intelligence should shrink its fee award. (Image from Shutterstock)

A federal appeals court has rejected an argument that a law firm’s use of artificial intelligence should shrink its fee award.

Reuters reported Monday that the 10th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals at Denver upheld a $115,000 fee awarded to defense lawyers at Brownstein Hyatt Farber Schreck by the lower court in a trade secrets dispute. The trial court had ruled that the fee was reasonable.

“Plaintiffs have not shown that defense counsel’s use of AI rendered the hours that ​they actually expended unreasonable,” wrote 10th Circuit Judge Carolyn McHugh for a unanimous three-judge panel.

The appeals court also upheld the ​dismissal of the lawsuit.

In her opinion, McHugh acknowledged that AI and similar research tools can make attorneys more efficient. But she stressed that lawyers must still verify legal authorities and arguments themselves.

According to Reuters, the case began in 2024, when industrial motor-efficiency equipment maker Flux Drive filed a suit against a Chinese manufacturer, alleging that one of its former engineers had stolen proprietary information and given it to them. After the case was dismissed, Flux Drive was ordered to pay the defendants’ legal fees. On appeal, the company argued that the defense billed for “ministerial tasks,” and that AI use should have lowered the bill.

The defendants countered that their lawyers checked every piece of AI-assisted research, and that Flux Drive pointed to no specific inflated entry, redundant task or unreasonable charge.

Brownstein Hyatt partner Christopher Ottele, who represented the defendants, called AI a powerful tool that sophisticated firms should embrace.

“This ​decision confirms that the use of AI is not a substitute for the judgment and analysis that attorneys still ​must exercise in every filing with the court,” Ottele told Reuters.

Counsel for the plaintiffs did not immediately respond to Reuters’ requests for comment.

#7608. Justice Kagan: firing point blank in Smith & Wesson v. Estados Unidos Mexicanos

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

In the 1983 movie A Christmas Story, Ralphie’s teacher, Miss Shields, assigns her students the task of writing “a theme.” The fourth-grade class at Warren G. Harding Elementary school erupts in groans; after all, writing is hard work.

But Ralphie sees it as an opportunity to make his case for a Red Ryder BB gun, “the Holy Grail of Christmas gifts.” And as the words “pour[] forth from [his] penny pencil with feverish fluidity,” he gets right to the point: “What I want for Christmas is a Red Ryder BB gun with a compass in the stock and this thing that tells time.”

Doubtless, Miss Shields had admonished her students – like our teachers admonished us – that each paragraph of a theme must begin with a thesis (or topic) sentence. But is that always right? Pay attention to skilled writers, and you’ll discover that – like many things – it depends.

Skilled writers do locate a paragraph’s issue (topic) and its point (thesis) where readers expect to encounter them. But readers have different expectations about where that should be. Sometimes readers expect the issue and the point in the first sentence, but sometimes they expect them to be separated. Readers change their expectations depending on what type of paragraph they are reading. And sometimes a paragraph has no point at all.

Justice Elena Kagan shows how this works. She never makes a reader hunt for her point, even though she might locate that point in different places for different types of paragraphs.

Take Smith & Wesson v. Estados Unidos Mexicanos as one of many potential examples. In Smith & Wesson, the court held that Mexico had failed to plead its way around a federal statute barring claims against gun manufacturers. Starting with meat-and-potatoes paragraphs, Kagan does exactly what Miss Shields might insist upon. She locates both the issue and the point of the paragraph right at the beginning, then uses the rest of the paragraph to prove her point.

In Section I.A. of the opinion, for example, Kagan sets out the requirements of the statute being interpreted, the Protection of Lawful Commerce in Arms Act. Taking only the first sentence of each paragraph, readers learn exactly how the statute works with zero effort. We read:

“[The PLCAA] bars cer­tain lawsuits against manufacturers and sellers of fire­arms.”

“But PLCAA’s general bar on those suits has an exception, usually called the predicate exception, relevant here.”

“Notably here, the predicate violation PLCAA demands may come from aiding and abetting someone else’s firearms offense.”

After each thesis, Kagan deploys the PLCAA’s language to prove that she’s right. For example, to prove that the PLCAA “bars certain lawsuits,” she quotes language providing that a “qualified civil liability action . . . may not be brought in any Federal or State court.” But again, before she shoves the reader’s nose into the language, she first tells us the point of it all.

In adopting this structure, Kagan is giving English readers what they expect. In his book “The Sense of Structure,” George Gopen calls these meat-and-potatoes paragraphs “medial paragraphs.” Here, in the middle of an exposition, “readers tend to appreciate being given the point up front.” Fail to put the point up front and one risks “having the reader disappear before the point actually arrives.” You run an especially grave risk if you are writing for busy legal readers – an audience that’s typically looking for a reason to stop reading.

But in other types of paragraphs, Kagan does not front-load a traditional thesis sentence, and she’s right there too. Consider the way Kagan writes introductions and narrative paragraphs.

In her Smith & Wesson introduction, Kagan reveals the issue or the topic in the first sentence, but she only gives the point or thesis in the last sentence. In the first sentence, we read that Mexico has sued American gun manufacturers – what the case is about. But before we can understand the court’s holding – the point – we need to learn some context. We need a sketch of what the law requires. So Kagan next sets out the statutory requirement: Mexico must plead that the gun manufacturers aided and abetted unlawful sales to the cartels. Only now, at the end of the paragraph, do we know enough to understand the point: Mexico did not plausibly plead aiding and abetting.

Again, according to Gopen, Kagan is satisfying her readers’ “remarkably fixed expectation that the point of an opening paragraph will arrive at the end.” We readers don’t want to be punched in the face with an answer before we know enough to understand it. Writers should make us “comfortable with the surroundings before we have to go to work.”

Narrative paragraphs involve yet another difference: readers don’t expect a traditional thesis in a passage that feels like “once upon a time.” Gopen notes, “Not all paragraphs were born to make a point.” Sometimes writers write “just to tell a story, to put some facts on the table.”

In her narrative paragraphs, Kagan sometimes just tells the story, and sometimes she fires a thesis point blank:

In the end, your old English teacher was mostly right. Ordinary, meat-and-potatoes paragraphs ought to have a sentence in which the issue and the point are together at the beginning of the paragraph. But specialized paragraphs might be different. So, before you start line-editing the sentences of a draft, employ a process to evaluate the strength of your paragraphs.

For your meat-and-potatoes paragraphs, prefer paragraphs that state the point and then prove it. Be on the lookout for paragraphs that write to a conclusion rather than stating it up front. To diagnose these paragraphs, try to create a reverse outline by copying the first sentence (sometimes two) into a different document. Ask yourself whether the argument makes sense with only those sentences. It will if the issue and point are stated up front.

In your statement of facts, mark which paragraphs have a thesis and which don’t. Know that you have a choice about when to include one, and make that choice.

Finally, give special attention to paragraphs that begin a text or a new section. Take the reader from the issue, through the necessary context, and then conclude with the point.

Why so much care? Because hitting the wrong target can be dangerous; you’ll shoot your eye out. A legal reader won’t just stand by trying to guess where the next round is being aimed.

Correction (Nov. 2 at 5:00 p.m.): A prior version of this article gave the case name as Smith & Wesson v. Estados Unidos de Mexico.

Professor Gray teaches legal writing courses for first-year and advanced students at Duke Law.

#7605. Is Montgomery affirmative action’s final chapter?

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

On Oct. 19, the Supreme Court granted cert in a case called Association for Education Fairness v. Montgomery County Board of Education. I am surprised it hasn’t received more press coverage because it could be the final nail in affirmative action’s coffin.

Perhaps you think the Supreme Court already hammered in that nail in Students for Fair Admissions, Inc. v. President & Fellows of Harvard College, but you’d be wrong. In that case, the court found racial preferences at Harvard and the University of North Carolina to be illegal. Nevertheless, many scholars are now urging schools to turn to what I call “race neutral affirmative action.” These are programs that seek to increase the number of some racial groups relative to others not by selecting for race itself, but by selecting for characteristics correlated with race. For example, instead of using race preferences in admissions, a university uses preferences for applicants who live in zip codes that are nearly all black, applicants who grew up on Indian reservations, or applicants for whom English is a second language. These are real-life examples of what some universities have done when they were forbidden from using race. Many affirmative action supporters think these sorts of things are perfectly legal.

But I have long argued that race proxies are just as illegal as using race itself. My arguments became moot points after the Supreme Court allowed universities to use race itself in admissions in the 2003 case of Grutter v. Bollinger. But now that SFFA has taken that off the table, the question I teed up is back in the limelight: is it constitutional to use racial proxies instead?

That’s what Montgomery County allegedly did to pick the students for its magnet middle schools. Its efforts predated SFFA because, even before the Supreme Court told universities not to use race, they had told school districts not to. In a nutshell, the alleged facts are these: Asian children make up only 15% of the school system’s population – it is majority black and Hispanic – but were taking up half the spots in the magnet middle schools. This didn’t go over well with many parents, so the school board sought to even things out. The board tried several plans but ultimately used a lottery among the applicants who scored above the 85th percentile in their neighborhood on standardized tests. Because the pool was based on how well applicants did compared only to others in their own neighborhood, the plan spread magnet school spots across the county – and, because many neighborhoods don’t have much racial diversity, it spread the spots across the races, too. The number of black and Latino students went up and the number of Asian students went down.

According to Supreme Court precedent, this is unconstitutional. We have a long history of attempts to discriminate indirectly when we couldn’t discriminate directly – and we have an equally long history of the Supreme Court telling us it’s illegal. For example, when we couldn’t deny the ability to vote on the basis of race, we tried using literacy tests and grandfather clauses and felon disenfranchisement instead. The court said those things are illegal. When we couldn’t segregate schools, we tried drawing school district boundaries around mostly black neighborhoods and mostly white neighborhoods instead. The court said we can’t do that, either.

The doctrine is this: if your “purpose” is to discriminate on the basis of race and your “effect” is to discriminate on the basis of race, then you are engaged in discrimination on the basis of race – even if you aren’t using a racial classification. It’s something like the old adage: if something walks like a duck and quacks like a duck, it’s a duck.

Most scholars supported these precedents when people were discriminating against blacks. But now not so much. Thus, I expect a bevy of amicus briefs from academics contorting their way through them. But the contortions I have seen thus far are very weak. For example, the leading theory on why these precedents don’t doom Montgomery County is the old distinction between “benign” and “invidious” discrimination: the purpose to help is different than the purpose to hurt. The precedents involved the purpose to hurt blacks, whereas Montgomery County was trying to help blacks (and Latinos); hurting Asians was just a byproduct, not the purpose.

If you thought the Supreme Court had already rejected – over and over again – the distinction between “benign” and “invidious” discrimination, you’d be right. After all, that’s how we got SFFA. As the court explained there, life is often zero-sum: if you help one race by giving them more spots, you necessarily hurt other races by giving them fewer spots. What is “benign” for one is “invidious” for the others. It’s a distinction without a difference.

The scholars say the cases rejecting the benign-invidious distinction don’t count because they involved racial classifications, not racial proxies. But the court in SFFA anticipated this move and cut it off: “[U]niversities may not simply establish through . . . other means the regime we hold unlawful today. … [W]hat cannot be done directly cannot be done indirectly. … The Constitution deals with substance, not shadows.” Yes, that’s dicta, but isn’t it very, very probative of what the very same justices will think about the very same question next year?

Moreover, the dicta didn’t come from nowhere: in fact, the Supreme Court has already struck down “benign” racial proxies – a bunch of them. When governments engage in racial gerrymandering of voting districts, they don’t use racial classifications: voters are assigned to one district or another based on where they live, not their skin color. Yet, even when these gerrymanders have been designed to help black and Latino voters, the Supreme Court has struck them down all the same, including just this past term in Louisiana v. Callais. Is not Montgomery County engaged in gerrymandering no less than Louisiana? It’s just school districts, not voting districts.

It is true that the court has required discriminators to try “race-neutral alternatives” before they can use race itself. But the court requires race-neutral alternatives only when discriminators otherwise have a compelling interest to justify their discrimination. All this means is that the court prefers racial proxies to racial classifications when forced to choose; it doesn’t mean racial proxies are insulated from constitutional scrutiny.

Still, the court may not need to get into all this because the question presented in the Montgomery County case merely asks what counts as a discriminatory “effect.” The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 4th Circuit held that the Asian students had to show a “disparate impact” – a term borrowed from Title VII law that means the challenged practice impacts one race more than another – and they couldn’t do so because, even after the gerrymandering, they still comprised a greater portion of the magnet school spots than they did of magnet school applicants.

Although it is true that disparate impact is one way to show a racial effect under the Supreme Court’s purpose-and-effect precedents, as I previously explained, it is not the only way. For example, when the Supreme Court said that school districts couldn’t evade its desegregation decrees by drawing district lines around mostly white neighborhoods and mostly black neighborhoods, it did not require the plaintiffs to show a disparate impact (e.g., schools of different quality); it was enough that one school was overwhelmingly white and the other was overwhelmingly black. When the Supreme Court has said that legislatures couldn’t gerrymander voting districts, it did not require the plaintiffs to show a disparate impact (e.g., differential vote dilution); it was enough that the racial composition of the districts had been affected.

It is true that what exactly the racial effect is in the voting cases is undertheorized. There is no obvious baseline to compare to the gerrymandered district lines in order to measure the “effect.” For this reason, some scholars think the court has all but read out the effect requirement from the purpose-and-effect test. Maybe so. The effect requirement comes from an old case called Palmer v. Thompson: there, Jackson, Mississippi, closed all their public swimming pools rather than desegregate them; the court held that this wasn’t unconstitutional racial discrimination because all the races had been affected equally. The ruling is unpopular among scholars on the left; law professor Randall Kennedy at Harvard has compared it to Korematsu. Thus, I doubt many will mourn its demise; plaintiffs would still have to show an injury to establish standing in federal court. But overruling it will only help the plaintiffs in the Montgomery County case.

Still, a lingering question that hasn’t been asked enough is whether the purpose-and-effect doctrine – or even a purpose-only doctrine if Palmer goes away – is consistent with the original understanding of the Constitution. It is hard for me to see how it couldn’t be: it is very easy to evade any rule by proxy; surely, they knew that even back in 1868. But I haven’t seen any historical analyses yet. I hope there are some in the briefing.

I appreciate that for many scholars it is inconceivable that we could end up in a world where it is illegal to do anything about racial disparities. Many of them endorse so-called “antiracism” and believe that all racial disparities must be the product of racism – and, indeed, that we, too, are racists if we don’t do something about them. This means we can sometimes have “too many” Asians. Maybe they’re right about that, maybe they’re wrong. But the 14th Amendment does not enact Mr. Ibram X. Kendi’s “How to Be an Antiracist.”

Brian Fitzpatrick was a law clerk to Antonin Scalia and is currently the Milton R. Underwood Chair in Free Enterprise and Professor of Law at Vanderbilt Law School.

Recommended Citation: Brian Fitzpatrick, Is Montgomery affirmative action’s final chapter?, SCOTUSblog (Nov. 2, 2026, 10:30 AM), https://www.scotusblog.com/2026/11/is-montgomery-affirmative-actions-final-chapter/

#7603. Trial opens for suspect whose multiple email threats include ‘skinning’ federal judge

A series of threatening emails sent to the Northern District of California last year included “skinning U.S. District Judge Charles Breyer” and accused judges from the Golden State of being “enemy combatants.” (Image from Shutterstock)

A series of threatening emails sent to the Northern District of California last year included “skinning U.S. District Judge Charles Breyer” and accused judges from the Golden State of being “enemy combatants.”

David Brooks Pokorny, 45, of El Cerrito, California, allegedly sent 11 email threats in a span of 44 minutes to assault, kidnap and murder Breyer, a senior judge for the Northern District of California, according to U.S. Assistant Attorney Kent Stejskal in opening statements Tuesday.

“Words within those 11 emails constitute what are called true threats,” said Stejskal, according to coverage by Courthouse News Service.

He allowed the 14-person jury to view snippets of the emails during the trial. Pokorny is charged with making felony threats against a judicial officer and faces a maximum sentence of 10 years in prison.

According to Pokorny’s public defender John Reichmuth, his client’s words were “truly shocking, truly offensive, truly ugly, but not true threats.”

Reichmuth said the emails were free speech, and the prosecution would have to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that Pokorny, who has a history of sending threats to public officials and media outlets, meant to perform the actions described in his emails.

Presiding U.S. District Judge Jon Tigar of the Northern District of California noted that the prosecution does not have to prove that Pokorny intended to carry out the threat for it to supersede the protections of First Amendment free speech rights.

#7600. Supreme Court declines Trump administration's request to intervene in California ballot dispute

In a brief, unsigned order released to reporters shortly before 6 p.m., however, the court turned down the government's request. There were no noted dissents.

In a 19-page filing, U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer requested an order from the justices that would require California to keep those ballots separate until the voters’ citizenship could be verified. “Once California commingles the challenged ballots with lawful ones,” Sauer wrote, “there is no way to get the challenged ballots back.”

The filing was the latest chapter in the Trump administration’s push to combat alleged voter fraud. It began last month, when the administration went to federal court in Los Angeles, seeking an order directing the state not to send ballots to, or count the ballots of, voters who were likely not citizens.

On Oct. 28, U.S. District Judge David Carter turned down the government’s request for a temporary order directing California to sequester the ballots of “likely noncitizens.” Among other things, he questioned the credibility of the Trump administration’s allegations that the voters it had identified were not U.S. citizens. On Friday, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit also rejected the Trump administration’s motion for emergency relief.

With the midterm elections now just one day away, the Trump administration sought relief next in the Supreme Court. Sauer argued that the government is likely to prevail on the merits of its claim – a key factor that courts consider in deciding whether to grant temporary relief – because federal law bars anyone who is not a U.S. citizen from voting in federal elections. Therefore, he wrote, “it follows that any ballot cast by an alien is unlawful” and states cannot count them.

The United States will also suffer permanent harm (another factor that courts consider in deciding whether to award temporary relief), Sauer continued, because “‘California admits that there is no way to trace a ballot after it is processed.’” The government’s “injury will continue to mount,” Sauer contended, “through Tuesday, November 10 (a week after election day, California’s deadline for receiving mail ballots.)”

By contrast, Sauer said, California will not suffer “undue hardship” from having to sequester the ballots at issue in this case. Indeed, he suggested, “California’s own election laws contemplate the segregation of challenged ballots, and the segregation of challenged ballots is a standard remedy in election cases.”

Sauer asked the court to also issue an immediate temporary order, known as an administrative injunction, “that requires California to segregate mail ballots from persons whom the United States has identified as likely noncitizens” while the justices consider the government’s request.

The Trump administration’s filing went first to Justice Elena Kagan, who has primary responsibility for emergency appeals from the 9th Circuit. Kagan then referred it to the full court, which declined the Trump administration’s request.

Amy Howe is the co-founder of SCOTUSblog and its primary reporter.

#7595. Virginia lawmakers assess misuse of automated license plate readers

Automated license plate readers have drawn backlash after reports of police abuse of the surveillance tech.

RICHMOND, Va. (CN) â Members of the Virginia General Assembly met Thursday to review a report on misuse of automated license plate readers by law enforcement agencies and the need for stronger guardrails.

âThe report, commissioned by the Virginia State Crime Commission, surveyed 191 local law enforcement agencies that reported using the controversial surveillance technology as of August. Of those, 10% self-reported unauthorized use of the technology, which uses a network of cameras to track vehicle movement.

âThe commission, comprised of legislators, commonwealth’s attorneys and appointed citizens, discussed the need for more guardrails.

â"It seems to me that we need probably stronger consequences for law enforcement agencies that are not following the laws that we pass," State Senate Majority Leader Scott Surovell, a Democrat, said at the meeting.

âRepublican Delegate Wren Williams discussed limiting access to the database to certified law enforcement employees. Hampton Commonwealth’s Attorney Anton Bell questioned whether those in his role should have discretion to bring charges against police for misuse. The criminal penalty for law enforcement is a class 1 misdemeanor, but prosecutors have charged only seven officers despite the report outlining numerous instances of misuse and noncompliance with state law.

Virginia-based state and federal courts have upheld the technology’s use in Fourth Amendment challenges. But criminal justice advocates and concerned Virginia residents used the public comment period to push for a complete ban.

â"There is no policing the police," Rob Poggenklass, representing the ACLU of Virginia, said. “While technology can be helpful to law enforcement, we cannot continue to hand over sensitive personal information such as location data to the highest bidder, and that’s exactly what’s happening with these surveillance technologies.”

âMitchell Smith, representing the Institute for Justice, echoed the sentiment and said his organization is pushing police to obtain warrants before using the database.

â"We do not surrender our constitutional rights when we leave our houses and go out in public," Smith said. “The best way to stop abuse is to prevent it from happening in the first place.”

âOf the 191 agencies that used ALPR technology at the time of the August survey, six reported not having an ALPR policy as state law requires. Of the 178 agencies that have policies, 33% do not publicly post their policy as required by law. Seven agencies reported data retention periods longer than the 21-day maximum allowed. In addition, 27 agencies acknowledged they did not engage in public awareness before implementing the technology in their communities.

âThe report also cited a May scientific article in Urban Science that outlined the higher concentration of Virginia’s ALPRs in areas with more of people of color. According to the commission, 42% of investigatory detentions resulting from ALPR-related stops between Jan. 1 and Sept. 30 involved Black people, despite only comprising 20% of the state’s population.

âTwenty-two agencies also reported their systems sometimes, or very often, produced false-positive hits. The report found agencies train officers to use the ALPR database in widely varying ways.

âVirginia enacted sweeping regulations in 2025 that limited permissible uses, mandated a 21-day maximum retention period, restricted data sharing and required monthly audits. Virginia’s regulations rank fourth on the NYU School of Law’s Policing Project’s license plate reader policy scorecard, losing points only for lacking a formal data-sharing process to ensure ALPR data sharing is lawful, authorized and documented.

âThe survey found 86% of agencies contracted with Flock Safety for their ALPR needs. Of the 191 responding agencies, 52 reported acts of vandalism ranging from people spray-painting the cameras, cutting power cables and purposefully hitting the cameras with vehicles. Vandals also set them on fire and shot the cameras, according to the report.

âDozens of Virginia localities have suspended, ended or decided not to renew their contracts with Flock Safety and other ALPR companies since responding to the August survey, including Alexandria, Arlington, Richmond and Lynchburg.

#7593. Minnesota high court urged to shield negative Google reviews from defamation suits

Though the underlying suit was tossed, the court will decide if such reviews qualify for increased free speech protections that speed up litigation and force losing plaintiffs to pay legal fees.

MINNEAPOLIS (CN) â Minnesota Supreme Court justices grappled Thursday with whether negative online business reviews should be awarded heightened free-speech protection against defamation suits.

While the reviewer, Robinet Productions LLC, paints the case as an attack on a small business owner attempting to warn others, the contractor, Paragon Restorations LLC, insists it is a simple dispute over unpaid, defective work that was weaponized to damage its reputation.

The feud stems from a failed commercial contract between the two parties. After Paragon refused to pay for promotional video work, Robinetâs owner posted a one-star Google review, claiming it was denied payment and urging others to avoid working with Paragon.

Paragon then sued Robinet, claiming defamation and arguing the review was false as the production company did not fulfill its contract obligations.

Robinet moved to dismiss the claim under Minnesotaâs Uniform Public Expression Protection Act â an anti-SLAPP statute designed to protect critics from âstrategic lawsuits against public participation,â which are âbaselessâ claims intended to silence speech through litigation.

âParagon never expected to win a monetary judgment,â Robinetâs attorney, Vince Reuter, said. âIt instead sought to punish Mr. Robinet for refusing to take down his business review, or through litigation, to force him to decide how much money he wanted to spend to protect his own free speech.â

Anti-SLAPP laws grant defendants fast-tracked judicial timelines, and granted motions force plaintiffs to pay attorneys fees and litigation expenses. Crucially, the act does not apply to purely private disputes, but rather âmatters of public concern.â

While the lower court notably dismissed Paragonâs defamation claim â finding the core statement that Robinet was denied payment technically true â it did so without applying the act, blocking the company from receiving attorneys fees.

The Minnesota Court of Appeals later agreed Robinetâs review was not a public concern â but rather a personal grievance based on a private transaction.

Robinet argues that reading cripples small business owners who lack the time and money required for litigation â noting the owner chose to forgo legal action in favor of an online review warning others against doing business with Paragon.

âThis Google review is an express warning to others,â Reuter said. âMr. Robinet used his experience to tell others about Paragonâs unprofessionalism and ultimate refusal to pay him anything for the hours of work that he provided.â

The Minnesota Supreme Court has an established constitutional test evaluating the content, form and context of a statement to determine whether it addresses a matter of public concern for First Amendment defamation purposes â which the lower courts use as a strict gatekeeper to evaluate anti-SLAPP protection.

Reuter argued this framework forces everyday consumer reviews through a system designed for high-stakes defamation, counter to the legislatureâs intent to protect public commentary.

âThe purpose of this law is to expand and broaden free speech,â he said.

Paragonâs attorney, Samuel Johnson, cautioned the court that opening the door to qualify business reviews as matters of public concern would bypass context and broaden the act’s intended reach.

âIf the legislature did what appellants say it would do, by making all ratings and reviews of businesses occupy that highest rung of First Amendment protection, that would invade the role of this court to decide what constitutional protections exist,â Johnson said, arguing the only purpose of the review was to express anger over unpaid services.

Justice Anne McKeig pushed back on Johnsonâs stance.

âIt seems the secondary purpose was to actually warn others,â she said, though Johnson argued there was no evidence anyone responded to Robinetâs review, meaning the speech had little to no social or political impact.

The bench was highly skeptical of this âcommunity connectionâ argument, questioning whether thatâs a fair way to measure impact or public concern.

âShould we be a little bit worried that weâre creating or adopting a test that sort of privileges popular statements and disadvantages unpopular statements?â Justice Karl Procaccini asked.

If the court sides with Robinet, negative online business reviews, consumer complaints and other warnings about bad business practices will have a clearer path for anti-SLAPP protection, which Robinet argued is essential.

âThe issue is, they get the advantage of these five-star reviews, but if somebody has the audacity to give them a one-star review on true facts and an honest and personal opinion, that person is dragged through the mud in a defamation claim,â Reuter said.

Justice Paul Thissen countered that a lot of people are harmed by defamation suits, but that may not necessitate heightened protection.

âIt could be that itâs really just, we want to protect those very highest levels of constitutional speech, and so the fact that maybe only 2% of business reviews are subject to the anti-SLAPP act may be exactly what the legislature intended,â he said.

Fulton Judicial Circuit District Attorney’s Office, Georgia, on whether an affirmative defense may be asserted as a basis for summary judgment if not presented earlier in a pleading.

On Monday afternoon, the court released its calendar for the January argument session, which will begin on Monday, Jan. 11. Learn about the session in the On Site section.

Today, the justices will hear argument in St. Mary Catholic Parish v. Roy, a religious discrimination challenge brought by Catholic preschools in Colorado over the state’s requirement that all schools participating in its universal preschool program must admit everyone – including LGBTQ children and children with LGBTQ parents.

Tomorrow, the justices will hear argument in Guerrero v. Johnson, on the limited circumstances in which a state prisoner can return to federal court for a second round of post-conviction review.

On Oct. 21, the Trump administration asked the justices to allow it to resume construction of its border wall in the Big Bend region of southwestern Texas. The request is now fully briefed, and the court’s decision could come at any time.

#7591. Texas asks Fifth Circuit to unblock law targeting companies that boycott fossil fuels

The state is seeking to lift an injunction issued by a federal judge who found the law violates the First Amendment by punishing companies for anti-oil and gas rhetoric.

(CN) â A Fifth Circuit panel Thursday wrestled with the constitutionality of a Texas law prohibiting the state from investing in or contracting with companies boycotting fossil fuels.

Senate Bill 13, passed in 2021, was the first major state law penalizing corporate climate initiatives. The law prohibits Texas’ retirement and school funds from investing in financial firms that boycott fossil fuel companies, and it also bans state contracts worth $100,000 or more with companies that boycott fossil fuels.

Texas is asking the Fifth Circuit to reverse a federal judge’s ruling that the law violates the First Amendment. U.S. District Judge Alan Albright, a Donald Trump appointee in the Western District of Texas, issued an injunction blocking the law in February, but a separate Fifth Circuit panel put that judgment on hold pending appeal.

On Thursday, the panel judges â all also Trump appointees â grappled with whether the law allows the state to punish companies for anti-oil and gas rhetoric.

The dispute comes down to a phrase in the statute saying a company is boycotting fossil fuels if it takes “any action that is intended to penalize” fossil fuel companies. Plaintiff American Sustainable Business Council, a coalition of businesses that advocate for sustainable practices, argues this includes anti-fossil fuel speech.

U.S. Circuit Judge Cory Wilson asked Beth Klusmann, a lawyer with the Texas Attorney General’s Office, about the plaintiff’s argument that the Texas Comptroller of Public Accounts has used the law to blacklist companies like major investment firm Blackrock for speech critical of fossil fuels, even though Blackrock still invests in fossil fuel companies.

Blackrock was initially added to Texas’ blacklist in 2022, but it was later removed after it withdrew from environmental initiatives like Climate Action 100+ that aim to reduce corporate greenhouse gas emissions.

Klusmann told the panel a company can be boycotting fossil fuels under the law’s definition while still investing in fossil fuel companies if it’s holding such companies to different standards.

“Think about it this way: In the context of, for example, a discrimination case under Title VII, you can hire women and still discriminate against them by holding them to higher standards, by paying them less, things of that nature,” she said. “You can still invest in fossil fuel companies but hold them to higher standards or require certain things of them that you don’t require from other investments. That would be considered penalizing under the statute, but it still falls within boycott, and it’s not focused on speech.”

The law exempts actions taken for “an ordinary business purpose.” Wilson questioned whether that phrase is unconstitutionally vague, as firms have been blacklisted despite providing commercial reasons for not investing in fossil fuels.

Klusmann responded that refusing to invest in a fossil fuel company because of environmental harm, rather than based on the financial viability of the company, would not be an “ordinary business purpose.” She returned to the comparison to Title VII.

“You can discriminate on the basis of sex if it is a bona fide occupational qualification, such as, for example, a sex-segregated locker room attendant,” she said. “Now, I couldn’t therefore say, well, I think women miss work more often because they stay home with their kids when they’re sick, and therefore that’s my bona fide occupational qualification. We can look through that and see, no, you’re just discriminating against women at that point. And so that’s what the comptroller is essentially trying to do here.”

The American Sustainable Business Council’s attorney, Rachel Nguemaha, argued excluding ordinary business purposes from the law’s definition of boycott is problematic because it “takes out commercial actions from the core of the definition, so you’re left with essentially a null set unless you include expressive activity.”

“Well, of course, there would be a problem if you didn’t put that in, right? Because then there could be any number of business decisions that would be eminently reasonable because you looked at P/E ratios or whatever, and you decided you weren’t going to invest in a particular asset class or a different particular group of securities, right?” U.S. Circuit Judge Andrew Oldham responded. “I mean, this is literally what business managers do all day, every day, is make decisions. We’re going to be long in this, short in that. We’re going to exclude this other thing. I mean, that’s the essence of being an investment advisor.”

The judges also pressed Nguemaha on Texas’ authority to regulate state investments.

“Why does the state have to join your boycott?” Wilson asked. “You’re saying that no matter what we do, that we have a right to compete for these funds and have state funds invested in our funds, regardless of whether we hurt the state.”

“It’s not no matter what we do,” Nguemaha responded. “It’s that the state cannot penalize companies on account of their protected expression.”

U.S. Circuit Judge Don Willett joined Wilson and Oldham on the panel. The judges took the case under submission and did not indicate when they would rule.

In a Phoenix courtroom, United Association National Pension Fund attorney Rachel Cocalis said the group has met all qualifications to certify the class of investors who lost money after Carvanaâs dramatic market plummets, and argued the retailer has not severed the link between price impacts and the specific misrepresentations it’s accused of.

Amid high inflation and rising interest rates coming out of the Covid-19 pandemic, âsurprisingly car sales went down,â Carvana attorney Peter Hammel told the court.

The parties did not disagree that the pension fund meets the standards necessary to represent a class: that the class is numerous, that there is a common question of law or fact, that the claims of the representative plaintiffs are typical of the class as a whole and that the representative plaintiffs will adequately protect the interests of the class.

But Hammel argued that no class period can be established because no more than one statistically significant stock price fluctuation occurred in the proposed period of May 2020 to October 2022.

Because Carvanaâs experts found only one statistically significant price fluctuation, there is no range of misdeeds to establish the beginning and end of a class period, he argued.

Representing the plaintiffs, Rachel Cocalis said a lack of statistical significance is not a death sentence for this type of claim if the defendants cannot prove a lack of causation.

The plaintiffs also accuse Carvana of lying about vehicle inspection standards and exaggerating its profit margins.

All the while, Carvana assured investors it was in compliance.

âBut Carvana continues its innocent until proven guilty approach despite knowing it would lead to DMV fines and loss of dealership access,â Cocalis said.

Defending Carvana, Hammel said the plaintiffs cannot prove that stock price changes had anything to do with statements made by Carvana.

The exception was Feb. 24, 2022, when stock price rose by 17%.

#7586. The border wall dispute isn’t fit for the emergency docket

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

In its latest request to the Supreme Court over President Donald Trump’s approach to immigration, the Justice Department turned to the court’s emergency docket to ask for fast-track permission to construct a border barrier system along a 517-mile stretch in remote west Texas. Stymied by a federal district court’s preliminary injunction issued in October, the Justice Department argues that Supreme Court intervention is needed to prevent irreparable harm to the country. But details of the government’s legal argument reveal that the Trump administration hopes to use the emergency docket as a fast track to victory regardless of the actual urgency of the legal dispute.

Early this year, the Department of Homeland Security began taking important preliminary steps to build physical barriers through Big Bend National Park, Big Bend Ranch State Park, and nearby property along the U.S.-Mexico border. Part of the Border Patrol’s Big Bend Sector, covering approximately one-quarter of the entire border, no artificial barriers exist there. Despite its massive geographic reach, the region is sparsely populated and at immense distance from large urban centers. Unlike other parts of the U.S.-Mexico border, few people or goods cross from one country to the other in the Big Bend Sector. Indeed, according to U.S. District Judge Kathleen Cardone, who issued a preliminary injunction blocking DHS from carrying out its plans to erect a border barrier in the area, this is the border region with “the lowest aggregate number of apprehensions [of migrants] and the lowest number of apprehensions per mile of border.”

In Mullin v. Friends of the Ruidosa Church, a group of individuals with personal or business ties to the region, along with two advocacy groups, argued that DHS had failed to comply with required environmental reviews. Pointing to a 1996 law signed by President Bill Clinton, the Justice Department responded that Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin and his predecessor, Kristi Noem, waived application of those environmental laws. The government also argued that the district court lacked the power to decide the lawsuit in the first place.

Cardone disagreed with the government on both counts. Congress narrowed courts’ jurisdiction in border-barrier disputes, but left room for courts to consider constitutional challenges to DHS’s conduct, she concluded. The challenge to Mullin’s waiver of environmental laws raises a constitutional question, Cardone added.

Having concluded that she could consider the challengers’ lawsuit, Cardone then turned to the criteria that Congress imposed on the secretary of Homeland Security to waive environmental review. The 1996 law directs the immigration agency “to waive all legal requirements” that could slow or impede construction of border barriers and roads. But the same law also instructs DHS to build barriers and roads “in areas of high illegal entry into the United States.” Considering the government’s data about apprehensions of people and seizures of drugs in the Big Bend Sector, as compared to other parts of the U.S.-Mexico border, Cardone concluded that the region cannot be considered to have high levels of illegal entry. “[I]f the Big Bend Sector is an area of high illegal entry, so is every other sector,” Cardone announced.

Seven days after Cardone released her opinion, the U.S. solicitor general asked the Supreme Court to intervene. Much of the government’s argument turns on its disagreement with Cardone about what constitutes an area of “high illegal entry.” Mullin determined that the Big Bend Sector constitutes an area of high illegal entry because Customs and Border Protection, the DHS agency that enforces immigration laws at and near the border, apprehended 89,000 people and “seized enormous amounts” of illicit drugs from fiscal years 2021 to 2025, the government explains. In addition, failure to build a border barrier in this region “would act as a dangerous magnet” for additional illegal entries, the solicitor general claims. Despite Mullin’s assessment that the facts on the ground met the “high illegal entry” threshold required by Congress, “the district court nonetheless issued an unprecedented injunction blocking those waivers and halting associated border-wall construction,” the solicitor general wrote to the court.

Unsurprisingly, the challengers disagree. Opposing the government’s request for relief from the justices, they describe Mullin and Noem’s waivers as “unprecedented” and claim they “carry undisputed and extraordinary political and economic significance.”

The solicitor general’s claim is fundamentally a dispute about the proper interpretation of the text of the 1996 law. The government argues that courts cannot second-guess Mullin’s decision to waive environmental laws, and that Mullin’s view of what constitutes “high illegal entry” is all that matters. Cardone disagrees and contends that courts have a role to play here.

By turning to the emergency docket, the Justice Department has dispensed with the ordinary appellate process in favor of a fast-track path to, it hopes, final victory. Wanting an answer sooner rather than later is understandable, but a party’s interest in “line-jumping,” as Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson has described the emergency docket, isn’t reason enough to circumvent the slower course of the ordinary appellate process. Jackson would prefer to limit the emergency docket to situations in which an actual emergency exists. It’s hard to see what exigency exists in west Texas, however. The solicitor general argues that drugs and people will continue to enter through the Big Bend Sector. That is undoubtedly true, but, as that stretch of land has been unfortified since it became a border on March 18, 1848, nothing is likely to occur in the near future that is markedly different from past decades.

The government’s request for fast-track intervention by the Supreme Court also does not meet the standards set by Jackson’s ideological opposites. Explaining his view of the court’s emergency docket in Trump v. CASA, the court’s fast-track decision announcing that district courts are not authorized to issue universal injunctions, Justice Brett Kavanaugh wrote that its alternative pathway is appropriate when “Congress passes a major new statute, or the Executive Branch issues a major new rule or executive order.” Neither applies to the border-wall dispute. Congress enacted the contested statute 30 years ago and the waivers issued by Mullin and Noem are neither an agency rule nor an executive order.

Nor is the border-wall legal battle the type of dispute that only the Supreme Court can resolve. In a 2021 speech, Justice Samuel Alito compared the court’s emergency docket to a hospital’s emergency room, suggesting that, in his view at least, the fast-track process is proper only when no suitable alternative exists. But an alternative does exist to decide if Cardone overstepped. The government could have appealed Cardone’s decision to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 5th Circuit. Like other circuit courts, the 5th Circuit regularly reviews preliminary injunctions granted by district courts. As Kavanaugh explained in CASA, “The courts of appeals and this Court can (and regularly do) expeditiously review district court decisions awarding or denying preliminary injunctive relief.”

It is true that Congress has made some challenges to the secretary of Homeland Security’s waiver authority reviewable by the Supreme Court. But it is not clear a dispute over what constitutes an area of high illegal entry fits that requirement. In a 2020 decision, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit explained that the language funneling appeals to the Supreme Court must be interpreted “narrowly.” That court then went on to consider a challenge to border-wall construction in south Texas. And the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit, in a case that the D.C. Circuit relied on favorably, distinguished a challenge to the secretary of Homeland Security’s power to waive laws from a challenge to the secretary’s authority to build barriers and roads. The 9th Circuit concluded that it could not review the secretary’s waiver but could review the secretary’s authority to order construction of a border barrier system. A case that “is related to or concerned with the Secretary’s waiver determinations” is not necessarily a challenge to the secretary’s waiver authority, the 9th Circuit explained.

Since Friends of the Ruidosa Church turns on the secretary’s authority to build barriers in areas of high illegal entry, and the government disagrees with Cardone’s interpretation of that section of the 1996 law, the 5th Circuit arguably is empowered to decide whether Cardone is correct. But instead of asking the 5th Circuit to correct the mistake it claims Cardone committed, the solicitor general skipped the 5th Circuit and went directly to the Supreme Court.

The reason it did this is not difficult to figure out: The administration is hopeful that it will receive a friendly audience at the Supreme Court. But this is a fast-track procedure meant for exceptional circumstances. And there is nothing exceptional about the legal fight over the administration’s attempt to build new segments of border barrier in rural west Texas. If the court grants the government’s request to pause Cardone’s preliminary injunction, allowing construction to move forward where no barrier currently exists, it should, at the very least, explain how this case meets the criteria that the justices have previously provided and if the term “emergency docket” is a misnomer.

A prior version of this article did not include the paragraphs beginning with “It is true that” and “Since Friends of the Ruidosa Church.”

César Cuauhtémoc García Hernández is the author of three books about immigration law and policy.

#7585. Airlines accused of sharing pricing data to inflate fares

Two airline passengers say seven major carriers used a shared database to monitor pricing and suppress fare competition.

(CN) â Seven major airlines used a shared database to monitor each other’s prices, curbing competition and driving up the cost of domestic air travel, two airline passengers claim in a proposed class action.

Ashley Ward and Gregory Morris sued the airlines, Airline Tariff Publishing Company and its subsidiary 3Victors on Wednesday in the U.S. District Court for the Western District of Washington. The plaintiffs claim the companies conspired to exchange confidential pricing information in violation of federal antitrust law.

The airline defendants include American, Delta, United, Southwest, Alaska, Hawaiian and JetBlue. Ward says she bought tickets from Southwest while Morris purchased flights from United, and both claim they paid artificially inflated fares.

At the center of the lawsuit are two products operated by 3Victors: Iris, an airline shopping and pricing data aggregator, and PriceEye, an analytics tool that lets airlines monitor competitorsâ fares and pricing changes.

The plaintiffs say airlines contribute shopping data and dynamically generated prices to Iris in exchange for access to PriceEye. The dashboard provides pricing alerts, competitive benchmarks and tools to detect unusual changes, allowing airlines to track rivalsâ pricing in near real time.

The arrangement operates on a âgive-to-getâ model. âParticipation in Iris is based on a simple principle: the more you contribute, the more you receive,â the plaintiffs say.

Ward and Morris say the system undermines the secrecy that dynamic pricing was supposed to bring to airline ticket sales. Airlines can use individualized offers to compete for customers, but sharing that information with competitors makes it easier to monitor and respond to price cuts.

3Victors advertises that PriceEye lets airlines âconfidently monitor the competitive landscape and adjust pricing strategies as markets shift â hour by hour, not day by day,â the plaintiffs say in the complaint.

They trace the arrangement to a working group called Airline Tariff Publishing Company, or ATPCO, formed in 2016 to study dynamic pricing. A study presented at an industry conference the following year illustrated how airlines unable to monitor one anotherâs private offers could engage in price wars, driving fares down.

ATPCO subsequently developed a system to standardize dynamic pricing data and began collecting airlinesâ shopping information. The company announced a program in 2023 that allowed airlines to analyze collective shopping data, and it acquired 3Victors later that year.

By 2025 and 2026, the plaintiffs say, ATPCO had integrated the technology into Iris and PriceEye, creating a system that allowed participating airlines to exchange and analyze sensitive pricing information.

The plaintiffs, represented by Steve W. Berman of Hagens Berman, seek to represent classes of domestic airline ticket purchasers. They want the court to block the information-sharing arrangement and award damages.

#7583. Will an ability to hold federal officers accountable survive this term?

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

At a time when there is a desire to hold ICE agents accountable for their constitutional violations, the Supreme Court might be poised to eliminate the only way to hold them civilly liable under federal law.

By way of background, if state or local officers violate the Constitution, they can be sued under a federal statute, 42 U.S.C. Section 1983. But no federal law authorizes suits against federal officers for constitutional violations. Rather, the ability to sue a federal government officer for money damages comes from a 1971 Supreme Court decision, Bivens v. Six Unknown Named Agents of the Federal Bureau of Narcotics. There, the court said that it would allow a cause of action for money damages under the Fourth Amendment even without a federal statute authorizing it.

Nevertheless, for decades, the Supreme Court has refused to extend or even apply Bivens to other violations of constitutional rights by federal officers, and several conservative justices have called for it to be overruled. Now, in Nielsen v. Watanabe, to be argued on Nov. 9, the court will again confront whether to allow a Bivens suit – and perhaps whether to end such claims entirely.

The underlying issue is about separation of powers: should the court provide a remedy for constitutional violations or is that entirely the province of Congress? But it also is about accountability: without Bivens, how can those who violate constitutional rights, including ICE agents, be held responsible and how can those injured be compensated?

Webster Bivens alleged that he had been subjected to an illegal and humiliating search by agents of the Federal Bureau of Narcotics. Bivens sought money damages as compensation for the harms he suffered. The court held that a federal law cause of action for money damages could be inferred directly from the Fourth Amendment. The majority, in an opinion by Justice William Brennan, emphasized that individuals whose rights have been violated should not be relegated to state law remedies, which might be inadequate or hostile to the federal constitutional interest.

In an important and often-cited concurring opinion, Justice John Marshall Harlan explained that the federal courts long have devised remedies for violations of federal law. Harlan said that it is essential that federal courts be able to provide such relief because “it is apparent that some form of damages is the only possible remedy for someone in Bivens’ alleged position. … For people in Bivens’ shoes, it is damages or nothing.” Harlan rejected the claim that the court violates separation of powers when it creates such a cause of action and remedy. In his view, the court is responsible for upholding and enforcing the Bill of Rights, and, hence, the judiciary need not wait for the legislature in order to act.

Chief Justice Warren Burger and Justices Hugo Black and Harry Blackmun dissented. Each wrote an opinion arguing that separation of powers means that Congress, and not the court, should create a cause of action for damages against federal officers. Black explained that “[s]hould the time come when Congress desires such lawsuits, it has before it a model of valid legislation, 42 U.S.C. §1983, to create a damage remedy against federal officers.” Similarly, Blackmun argued that “it is the Congress, and not this Court, that should act.”

For a decade after Bivens, the court applied and extended it. In 1979’s Davis v. Passman, the court allowed a Bivens suit under the due process clause of the Fifth Amendment for an equal protection claim. Congressman Otto Passman fired his administrative assistant, Shirley Davis, because he wanted a male to fill the position. In allowing the suit against the congressman, the court emphasized the judiciary's role in ensuring effective protection of constitutional rights.

And only a year later, in Carlson v. Green, the court allowed a Bivens suit for violation of the Eighth Amendment. A mother sued federal prison officials on behalf of her deceased son, claiming that he was the victim of gross inadequacies of medical facilities and staff, which caused his death and constituted cruel and unusual punishment. A remedy was available under the Federal Tort Claims Act; thus, the issue before the court was whether a Bivens suit should be allowed in light of this alternative. The court concluded that Bivens suits were a “counterpart” to the Federal Tort Claims Act because the act creates liability for the federal government and a Bivens cause of action permits recovery from federal officers themselves. The court found no indication that Congress intended for the act to preclude Bivens suits.

Since 1980, however, the court has not ruled in favor of a Bivens claim. In its most recent decision about Bivens, 2022’s Egbert v. Boule, the court noted that it had “declined 11 times to imply a similar cause of action for other alleged constitutional violations” and that “in all but the most unusual circumstances, prescribing a cause of action is a job for Congress, not the courts.”

Specifically, the court has held that that such claims are not allowed if there is a statute that precludes suits (in 2010’s Hui v. Castaneda), or that provides an alternative remedy even if it is inadequate (in 1988’s Schweiker v. Chilicky). It has precluded Bivens claims for those injured while in the military, even for egregious violations of their rights (in 1987’s United States v. Stanley). It has ruled that Bivens suits should be allowed only if they are on balance desirable and consistently has found that they are not (in 2007’s Wilkie v. Robbins, 2017’s Ziglar v. Abbasi, 2020’s Hernandez v. Mesa, and Boule). And it has precluded Bivens suits against private prisons that contract with the federal government (in 2001’s Correctional Services Corp. v. Malesko) and the guards employed by them (in 2012’s Minecci v. Pollard).

Based on this line of cases, the court in Egbert v. Boule stressed that recognizing a Bivens cause of action “is ‘a disfavored judicial activity.’” The court stated that

The court then laid out the framework for Bivens claims going forward. According to the majority, this should be guided by a two-step inquiry:

This is a test that puts a very strong presumption against recognizing Bivens claims.

Like Carlson v. Green, Nielsen v. Watanabe involves an Eighth Amendment claim for cruel and unusual punishment.The case involves a prisoner, Kekai Watanabe, who alleges that he suffered a broken tailbone when attacked by other prisoners that caused him excruciating pain and that a staff nurse, Francis Nielsen, denied him medical care. The court granted review as to whether the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit “erred [here] in recognizing a Bivens cause of action.”

Watanabe argues to the court that this case is governed by Carlson v. Green and does not seek to extend Bivens in any way. His brief states: “Watanabe asserts the same kind of violation of the same constitutional right by the same type of defendant in the same institutional setting pursuant to the same substantive standards as the plaintiff in Carlson. This is precisely the kind of claim this Court has long understood Carlson to encompass.”

In response, Nielsen argues that Bivens suits are strongly disfavored and that there are “significant factual differences such as the immediacy and severity of the harm alleged” compared with Carlson. But that is not all: Nielsen also expressly argues that “Bivens should be overruled” and that “Congress, not the judiciary, creates causes of action.”

The court could affirm the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit and allow a Bivens suit, saying that this is governed by Carlson. Or the court could distinguish Carlson, accepting Nielsen’s argument that there are sufficient factual differences between the cases, essentially limiting Bivens claims only for cruel and unusual punishment claims involving deaths. Or the court could overrule Carlson but not overrule Bivens.

Or the court could overrule Bivens entirely, which several conservative justices have advocated in the past.

The fundamental disagreement, as it was in Bivens, is whether it is the judicial role to provide remedies for violations of constitutional rights or whether that is just for Congress. The practical reality is that without Bivens suits, those whose rights have been violated – even horribly – are left with no recourse. In Hernandez v. Mesa, for example, a boy in Mexico was killed by shot fired across the border by a federal agent in Texas. The court’s rejection of a Bivens suit left no remedy at all.

In that case, and in many other situations, the Federal Tort Claims Act does not allow suits against the United States. Often there are not state tort remedies available either. To paraphrase Justice Harlan, for people in the shoes of many injured by federal officers, it is Bivens suits or nothing.

I would like to think that the reports of egregious constitutional violations by ICE agents, including killings, would cause the court to realize the importance of Bivens suits and to not end such causes of action. That is what makes Nielsen v. Watanabe so important.

Erwin Chemerinsky is the Dean and Jesse H. Choper Distinguished Professor of Law, University of California, Berkeley School of Law.

AUSTIN, Texas (CN) â Texas Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa made her first appearance Thursday after her stunning electoral victory over Greg Abbott.

At the LBJ School of Public Affairs at the University of Texas at Austin, Hinojosa unveiled the leaders of her transition team and sought to set the tone for what Texans can expect from her administration, telling reporters, âNow the fun part starts.â

âWe will have a bipartisan transition, and we will have a bipartisan administration and government in Texas,â Hinojosa said.

Joe Madden, a public affairs consultant from Houston, is heading up her transition team and will serve as its executive director. The team also includes Ryan Pollock, head of the Texas Building Trades Council and a labor union leader, as well as Ernest Bailes, who introduced himself as a conservative Republican honored to work with the governor-elect.

âI believe in Gina, and I have faith that we will be able to do good things for the state of Texas,â Bailes said. âWe will put partisanship aside. We will work together for what is best for the kids of the state of Texas.â

Hinojosa highlighted a few of her priorities during her brief remarks, among them addressing affordability, ending the culture of divisive politics and supporting public education. She also said the outgoing Abbott administration has been gracious by fully committing to a smooth transition of power.

When Hinojosa assumes office on Jan. 19, 2027, she will wield power that has been out of reach of Democrats for a generation. âUnchecked executive emergency powers, which, if not revoked, guarantee that Gina Hinojosa assumes not just the powers our state constitution bestows upon a governor, but will, in effect, inherit nearly all the powers of a dictator,â Harrison wrote in a letter to Abbott penned the day after the election.

Hinojosa was asked about Harrisonâs blunder during Thursdayâs conference, to which she responded: âThe people of Texas have spoken.â

âI think it’s important that as elected leaders we respect what the people of Texas have said,â Hinojosa explained. âThey want change, and I would hope that elected leaders from both parties don’t get in the way of the progress we can make together to deliver for working people.â

As of Thursday afternoon, Hinojosa leads Abbott by seven points, a bruising defeat for the longtime governor who was seeking a fourth term in office.

Political pundits, lawmakers and Texans are still in a state of reeling after Tuesdayâs historic election. The Lone Star State, previously seen as the Republicansâ crown jewel, flipped entirely, with all statewide offices breaking for Democrats. In addition, Democrat state lawmaker James Talarico bested Republican Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton to become the stateâs first Democrat elected to the U.S. Senate since 1988.

In a poignant post on X, Texas Senator Ted Cruz shared his thoughts on the stateâs dramatic political change.

âTexas is blue,â Cruz wrote. âThat is a hard sentence to utter. But Texas, today at least, is blue. As we sit here today, I am the only statewide elected Republican who remains in Texas. Thatâs not something I ever thought I would say.â

#7579. This state senator wrote music for ‘Dragon Ball Z;’ will he go ‘Super Saiyan’ as new Texas AG?

“Dragon Ball Z,” a popular animation series, has musical scores written by Texas lawyer and state Sen. Nathan Johnson, D-Dallas, who was recently elected as the state’s new attorney general. (Image from Shutterstock)

Before Texas state Sen. Nathan Johnson, D-Dallas, unleashed a “blue spirit bomb” on opponent Mayes Middleton on Tuesday night in the midterm elections for the Texas attorney general spot, the Thompson Coburn lawyer composed musical scores for Dragon Ball Z, a Japanese anime series about martial artists who defend the world from destruction.

Johnson, who got at least 52% of the vote and is a Dallas lawyer, will be the first Democrat to serve as the Texas attorney general in more than 30 years, Chron.com reports.

The show introduced various terms to the United States, including “Super Saiyan,” which means getting a huge surge of physical strength and hair that stands straight up, and “blue spirit bomb,” which is something released on opponents during an attack.

A piano player, Johnson learned how to write music while working as a lawyer and liked it so much that he decided to quit his job and focus on doing film and television composition, according to the article.

Johnson eventually went back to law and started a solo practice. While looking for office space, he met a landlord connected to a Texas company that licensed the English version of Dragon Ball Z in the United States. The company then hired Johnson in the early 2000s, according to Chron.com.

“It gave me a creative outlet and a cultural connection that very few people have had the opportunity to have,” Johnson said in an interview, according to Variety.
